strengths: Introduces two well-formalized metrics (SRP and SCH) for local routing consistency, with rigorous derivations and proofs (Appendix C) showing SRP has a closed-form optimal solution independent of any specific caching heuristic.

Large-scale empirical study spanning 20 diverse MoE LLMs (3B-57B parameters, encoder-decoder and decoder-only, various expert-count/sharing configurations), which is unusually broad for this type of analysis paper and lends credibility to the architectural conclusions.

The two proposed metrics are shown to be highly correlated with each other and with the hit rates of practical caching algorithms (LRU, LFU, Fixed-cache), helping justify that the idealized metrics are relevant to real deployment scenarios.

Provides concrete, actionable design guidance for practitioners (avoid shared experts, apply MoE at every layer, use cache sizes about 2x active experts) that could directly inform future MoE architecture and offloading-system design.

Extensive appendix analyses (base vs. post-trained models, perplexity correlation, positional stability, domain transitivity, layer-wise and expert-wise breakdowns, bootstrap confidence intervals) substantially strengthen empirical rigor and robustness of the main claims.

The connection identified between local routing consistency, load balance, and domain-specialized experts is a nuanced and non-obvious finding beyond a simple 'sparser routing implies more locality' narrative.
weaknesses: The central architectural findings (every-layer MoE, no shared experts correlate with higher SRP/SCH) are purely observational across pre-existing models that differ simultaneously in many confounded factors (training data, model size, expert ratios, training recipe); no controlled ablation training matched models is performed to establish causality.

All caching metrics are computed under an oracle/idealized setting with full knowledge of future activations within a segment; although correlation with LRU/LFU/Fixed-cache hit rates is reported, no actual expert-offloading system is implemented to measure realistic end-to-end deployment metrics such as latency or throughput on memory-constrained hardware, weakening the practical deployment claims.

The recommended cache-size ratio of about 2x active experts is derived from an informal visual 'turning point' argument in SCH curves rather than a rigorous cost-benefit optimization accounting for real memory/latency trade-offs.

Main-paper figures are extremely dense multi-panel scatter and bar plots with many overlapping tiny markers and abbreviated model labels, making them hard to parse without repeated referral to appendix tables.

The paper does not quantitatively benchmark its proposed SRP/SCH metrics against simpler existing locality measures used in prior expert-offloading works (e.g., next-token same-expert probability), so the added value over simpler metrics is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Segment-based routing/caching assumes a single fixed expert group for an entire segment, a stylized abstraction that may not fully reflect more flexible real-world caching policies, potentially limiting transferability of the reported optimal ratios to more sophisticated offloading systems.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem (expert offloading for memory-constrained MoE deployment) with a large-scale empirical study spanning 20 MoE LLMs of diverse sizes, architectures, and training regimes.

Proposes two formally defined metrics (SRP and SCH) with rigorous derivations of their optimal solutions (Appendix C proofs), giving the work a degree of theoretical grounding beyond ad hoc heuristics.

Validates that the oracle-based SCH metric correlates strongly with real cache algorithms (LRU, LFU, fixed cache), which helps justify that the idealized metric is a reasonable proxy for practical systems.
Provides a reasonably thorough set of ablations: base vs. post-trained models, per-layer and per-position analysis, domain-wise breakdowns, and expert-level specialization analysis.

Derives a concrete, potentially actionable guideline (cache size ~2x active experts) that could inform system design, and identifies architectural correlates (MoE-every-layer, no shared experts) associated with higher local routing consistency.
weaknesses: The central architectural claims (every-layer MoE and no shared experts yield higher consistency) are drawn from observational correlation across heterogeneous, uncontrolled models that differ simultaneously in training data, scale, and training recipes; no controlled ablation (e.g., training matched models with/without shared experts) is provided to support a causal interpretation.

All findings are based on oracle/idealized segment-level metrics computed post hoc on collected routing traces; there is no end-to-end evaluation of an actual expert-offloading system (latency, throughput, memory footprint) to confirm that the identified 'consistency' translates into real deployment gains.

The four-way grouping of models (Groups 1–4) and several other conclusions (e.g., the 2x cache-size sweet spot, domain vs. vocabulary specialization dominance) appear to be derived largely by visual inspection of scatter/line plots rather than principled statistical clustering or hypothesis testing, weakening the rigor of the conclusions.

Several claimed patterns have notable exceptions acknowledged in the text (e.g., Qwen3/GRIN-MoE breaking the load-balance vs. consistency tradeoff, LLaMA-MoE-v2/Qwen2 lacking domain specialization yet fitting other narratives), which undercuts the generality and predictive power of the proposed design principles.

Segment lengths are capped at 256 tokens, leaving open how well the conclusions generalize to longer-context or streaming generation scenarios that are often the primary motivation for expert offloading.

The paper does not compare SRP/SCH against simpler existing consistency measures (e.g., the 2-token consecutive-activation statistic from Jiang et al. 2024) to demonstrate that the added complexity of the proposed metrics yields meaningfully better or more actionable insights.

The practical takeaway for practitioners choosing or designing models for offloading remains somewhat vague, since the paper offers correlational architectural associations rather than a validated, prescriptive design methodology or a demonstrated speedup on real hardware.

strengths: Introduces two well-motivated, theoretically grounded metrics (SRP and SCH) for quantifying local routing consistency in MoE models, with formal definitions and proofs (F1-optimality of segment routers) in the appendix, giving the work rigor beyond a purely empirical study.

Extensive empirical scope: 20 diverse real-world MoE LLMs spanning 3B-57B parameters and multiple architectures (token-choice, expert-choice-like, encoder-decoder, shared-expert, hybrid SSM), plus a systematic ablation suite of pretrained toy models (TOY) that isolates individual architectural/training factors (load balance coefficient, shared experts, expert granularity, dense/sparse layer placement, top-k).

Findings are actionable and non-trivial for practitioners: e.g., the trade-off between local and global load balance, the negative effect of shared experts on local routing consistency, and the empirically grounded recommendation of cache size ≈2x active experts, which is directly useful for MoE architecture/deployment design.

Good methodological care: checks base vs. post-trained model differences, positional effects on SRP, correlation between SCH and realistic cache algorithms (LRU/LFy), and even a follow-up throughput study connecting the abstract metrics to real system overhead (Appendix F), which strengthens the practical relevance of the proposed metrics.
Thorough domain/vocabulary specialization analysis linking routing consistency to interpretability of expert specialization, adding scientific insight beyond just the systems-oriented motivation.
Clear diagrams (SRP/SCH illustrations) and reasonably comprehensive appendices support reproducibility; the paper commits to releasing code and sampled corpus.
weaknesses: The throughput validation (Appendix F) is only briefly described with correlation coefficients (r≈0.2, r≈-0.3) and no detailed experimental setup, plots, or statistical rigor, making it hard to fully verify the claimed connection between the proposed metrics and real-world system performance, which is the paper's ultimate motivating scenario.

The grouping of REAL models into four qualitative SRP-based clusters (Group 1-4) is somewhat ad hoc/subjective, and some conclusions (e.g., domain specialization link with SRP) have notable exceptions (Qwen2, LLaMA-MoE-v2) that are explained post-hoc rather than predicted.

TOY models are relatively small (1.43B parameters, 8 layers, trained on only 20B tokens) compared to the large REAL models under study; it is unclear how well conclusions from these toy-scale ablations generalize to much larger, more heavily trained production MoE models.

The recommendation of cache ratio ρ≈2 is derived mainly from visual 'turning point' inspection of SCH curves (Fig. 8) for only a subset of models (Group 1), rather than a more rigorous optimization criterion across the full diverse model set, weakening the generality of this headline practical recommendation.

Some interacting confounds among architectural factors (e.g., shared experts vs. reduced combination space, dense layers vs. shared experts in DeepSeek family) are only partially disentangled, as the authors themselves note for Phi/GRIN not following the combination-space trend.

The paper is dense with many metrics, figures, and heuristics, and the core practical takeaways (avoid shared experts, use ~2x cache ratio, some load imbalance is fine) could be more crisply summarized/foregrounded relative to the very extensive analysis, somewhat limiting accessibility to a broader systems audience.
